subareas.name: Government as a Platform / GOV.UK core platform

sources.name: GDS blog
sources.why: Official Government Digital Service blog: GOV.UK One Login, GOV.UK app, Service Standard evolution — the heart of the platform subarea.

sources.name: CDDO blog
sources.why: Central Digital and Data Office — cross-government digital/data strategy, legacy IT modernisation and the '20 systems' mission.

sources.name: PublicTechnology
sources.why: UK govtech trade press covering GDS moves, One Login rollout, central digital programmes and platform decisions.

sources.name: State of Digital Publishing
sources.why: Independent senior-digital-leader blog on service design, content strategy and publishing practice inside public-sector and health organisations.

sources.name: PublicTechnology (service design coverage)
sources.why: Reports service standard evolution and user-centred design adoption across government departments.

sources.name: Institute for Government
sources.why: IfG publishes landmark reports and commentary on digital transformation of public services and management of digital government.

sources.name: Civil Service blog
sources.why: Civil Service Leadership blog tracks DDaT profession, digital capability framework and transformation programmes across departments.

sources.name: The Register — Public Sector
sources.why: Independent tech press with dedicated public-sector coverage: legacy IT failures, digital identity rollout and Whitehall tech projects.

sources.name: GDS blog (One Login updates)
sources.why: Authoritative for GOV.UK One Login / GOV.UK Verify replacement programme details and digital identity rollouts.

sources.name: PublicTechnology
sources.why: Tracks political and policy decisions affecting the national digital identity rollout.

sources.name: PublicTechnology (local government)
sources.why: Covers council digital transformation and shared-services programmes.

sources.name: Socitm (Society for Innovation, Technology and Modernisation)
sources.why: UK membership body for public-service technology leaders — council digital transformation, service design and shared-services analysis from the local government perspective.

sources.name: Digital Luton
sources.why: Council digital team blog with working RSS — practical service design and digital delivery lessons from local government.

sources.name: FedScoop
sources.why: US federal government tech news: digital platform strategy, FedRAMP, govtech modernisation and AI adoption — direct US comparison to UK GDS, with a working RSS feed.

sources.name: Chosen Path (Owen Boswarva)
sources.why: Long-running independent commentary on UK government data policy, transparency and FOI — first-principles analysis of data infrastructure.

sources.name: Data in government (GDS/analysis)
sources.why: GDS data science and analysis team blog — practical data policy, performance analysis and data sharing inside government; working RSS feed replacing the bot-blocked ODI for this subarea.

registries.name: GOV.UK Find and update open data
registries.why: Official UK government open data portal — machine-readable datasets on public services, spend and transformation.

registries.name: GOV.UK Digital Marketplace (G-Cloud / DOS)
registries.why: National registry of digital services and frameworks — reveals government's supplier ecosystem for platform and service delivery.

registries.name: ONS
registries.why: Office for National Statistics data on government digital service uptake, internet use and digital inclusion baselines.

registries.name: OpenAlex
registries.why: Open scholarly index API for discovering peer-reviewed research on digital government, e-gov and public-sector innovation.

notes: UK-centric per the topic's `in` scope (DWP/HMRC/GDS/design systems). Subscribed blog.gov.uk domains (GDS platforms, Policy Lab, user research, department digital teams) are blacklisted; the GDS main blog and CDDO blog are distinct non-blacklisted domains and are retained as core signals. Trade press falls back to free headline feeds (crawl_root given) for paywalled articles. Topic's 'out' boundaries respected: no party politics or general public-services commentary.
